title: Virtual Medical Appointment Systems
desc: Set up and run an online appointment system for a clinic: booking, identity, consent, records, reminders and fall-back plans.
outcomes: Describe the full patient journey from booking to follow-up.
Configure booking slots, reminders and consent steps.
Find failure points such as no-shows and poor connections.
Judge privacy and security of a tool.
Launch a pilot with a service level and review.
task: Design and pilot a virtual appointment flow for one small clinic, with booking, identity check, consent, reminders, records and a fall-back for failed calls.
condition: A practice clinic or case, a free booking tool, a spreadsheet, two peers and a clinic mentor. Real patient data is not used.
standard: Flow works end to end in 10 mock appointments; ID and consent are recorded; failed-call fall-back works within 10 minutes; privacy checklist passes; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Clinic managers, receptionists, nurses, health-IT beginners.
evidence: flow diagram, tool settings, 10 mock appointment log, privacy checklist, pilot review
modules: The patient journey
Understand

Request, book, remind, join, identify, consent, consult, record, follow up.
Mark who does each step: patient, front desk, clinician, system.
Add a way for patients with no smartphone.
A clinic adds phone-in booking for older patients, so 20% more elderly patients attend.
Draw your journey map.
All nine steps have an owner.
Booking and reminders
Apply
Good booking reduces no-shows.
Slots by clinician, length and type; buffer time between visits.
Reminders by message the day before and one hour before.
Cancel and reschedule in two taps.
A clinic cuts no-shows from 18% to 9% with two reminders.
Configure slots and reminders in a practice tool.
Test booking works with 5 mock patients.
Identity and consent
Apply
Know who is on the call and that they agree.
Check name and date of birth; for minors, a guardian.
Ask consent for the video, notes and any recording.
Record consent in the visit file.
The clinician says: "Please confirm your name and birth date. Are you happy to have this visit by video?"
Write a consent script.
Script covers identity, visit by video, notes and privacy.
Technology and connection
Analyse
Failures are normal; plan for them.
Test link, camera, mic and speed before the visit.
If video fails, switch to voice, then phone, then rebook.
Keep a technical help number.
A test call finds the patient's microphone is muted; a 2-minute fix.
Write a three-step fall-back and run it twice.
Fall-back restores contact within 10 minutes.
Privacy, security and records
Evaluate
Health records are the most sensitive data.
Strong passwords, two-step sign-in, encrypted storage and access logs.
Share only with those who need it; follow local health-data rules.
Never use public chat tools without approval.
A receptionist loses access because she shared a password; policy now bans sharing.
Complete a privacy and security checklist for your tool.
No item fails without a fix plan.
What virtual care cannot do
Evaluate
Some problems need an in-person visit.
Emergencies, physical exams, tests and procedures.
Clear rules for when to refer in person.
Teach patients what to do if worse.
Chest pain is sent to emergency care, never handled by video.
Write five red-flag rules agreed with a clinician.
Clinician mentor approves the rules.
Access and fairness
Analyse
Not everyone has the same tools.
Offer phone, large-text and language options.
Support low-bandwidth modes and shared community points.
Track who does not attend and ask why.
A rural clinic uses a village centre with a tablet and a helper.
List three barriers and fixes.
Each barrier has a fix and an owner.

Run 10 mock visits; measure wait, success, satisfaction.
Fix top problems; set a target such as 90% of calls start on time.
Plan monthly reviews.

Present your pilot review.
Numbers are real and a next step is dated.
quiz: Name four steps in the journey.
Booking, reminder, ID check, consent, consult, record, follow-up. (Covered in module 1: The patient journey. To pass that module: All nine steps have an owner.)
Why two reminders?
They cut no-shows. (Covered in module 2: Booking and reminders. To pass that module: Test booking works with 5 mock patients.)
What do you check before video visits?
Identity and consent. (Covered in module 3: Identity and consent. To pass that module: Script covers identity, visit by video, notes and privacy.)
What is the fall-back order?
Voice, phone, then rebook. (Covered in module 4: Technology and connection. To pass that module: Fall-back restores contact within 10 minutes.)
Name two security measures.
Two-step sign-in and encrypted storage. (Covered in module 5: Privacy, security and records. To pass that module: No item fails without a fix plan.)
Name a case not for video.
Emergency such as chest pain. (Covered in module 6: What virtual care cannot do. To pass that module: Clinician mentor approves the rules.)
Why keep access logs?
To show who saw a record. (Covered in module 7: Access and fairness. To pass that module: Each barrier has a fix and an owner.)
Name one access fix.
Phone option or community point. (Covered in module 8: Pilot and improve. To pass that module: Numbers are real and a next step is dated.)
What is a pilot target example?
90% of calls start on time. (Covered in module 8: Pilot and improve. To pass that module: Numbers are real and a next step is dated.)
Who approves red-flag rules?
A clinician. (Covered in module 8: Pilot and improve. To pass that module: Numbers are real and a next step is dated.)

ladder: The patient journey

L1: learner can name the steps of a patient visit. Focus module: The patient journey (Understand, 3 h). Map every step so none is forgotten. Key points: Request, book, remind, join, identify, consent, consult, record, follow up. Mark who does each step: patient, front desk, clinician, system. Add a way for patients with no smartphone.

Teach: open with the worked example. A clinic adds phone-in booking for older patients, so 20% more elderly patients attend. Then set the activity: Draw your journey map. Mark against the standard: All nine steps have an owner. Check at this level: Name four steps in the journey. Model answer: Booking, reminder, ID check, consent, consult, record, follow-up. Use a drawing.
Booking and reminders

L2: learner knows why consent and privacy come first. Focus module: Booking and reminders (Apply, 4 h). Good booking reduces no-shows. Key points: Slots by clinician, length and type; buffer time between visits. Reminders by message the day before and one hour before. Cancel and reschedule in two taps.

Teach: open with the worked example. A clinic cuts no-shows from 18% to 9% with two reminders. Then set the activity: Configure slots and reminders in a practice tool. Mark against the standard: Test booking works with 5 mock patients. Check at this level: Why two reminders? Model answer: They cut no-shows. Explain consent.
Identity and consent

L3: learner can set up booking and reminders. Focus module: Identity and consent (Apply, 4 h). Know who is on the call and that they agree. Key points: Check name and date of birth; for minors, a guardian. Ask consent for the video, notes and any recording. Record consent in the visit file.

Teach: open with the worked example. The clinician says: "Please confirm your name and birth date. Are you happy to have this visit by video?" Then set the activity: Write a consent script. Mark against the standard: Script covers identity, visit by video, notes and privacy. Check at this level: What do you check before video visits? Model answer: Identity and consent. Practise on a free tool.
Technology and connection

L4: learner can run a mock virtual visit. Focus module: Technology and connection (Analyse, 4 h). Failures are normal; plan for them. Key points: Test link, camera, mic and speed before the visit. If video fails, switch to voice, then phone, then rebook. Keep a technical help number.

Teach: open with the worked example. A test call finds the patient's microphone is muted; a 2-minute fix. Then set the activity: Write a three-step fall-back and run it twice. Mark against the standard: Fall-back restores contact within 10 minutes. Check at this level: What is the fall-back order? Model answer: Voice, phone, then rebook. Role-play a failed call.
Privacy, security and records

L5: learner can review tools and measure a pilot. Focus module: Privacy, security and records (Evaluate, 4 h). Health records are the most sensitive data. Key points: Strong passwords, two-step sign-in, encrypted storage and access logs. Share only with those who need it; follow local health-data rules. Never use public chat tools without approval.

Teach: open with the worked example. A receptionist loses access because she shared a password; policy now bans sharing. Then set the activity: Complete a privacy and security checklist for your tool. Mark against the standard: No item fails without a fix plan. Check at this level: Name two security measures. Model answer: Two-step sign-in and encrypted storage. Share numbers.
Access and fairness

L6: learner can coordinate a small clinic desk. Focus module: Access and fairness (Analyse, 3 h). Not everyone has the same tools. Key points: Offer phone, large-text and language options. Support low-bandwidth modes and shared community points. Track who does not attend and ask why.

Teach: open with the worked example. A rural clinic uses a village centre with a tablet and a helper. Then set the activity: List three barriers and fixes. Mark against the standard: Each barrier has a fix and an owner. Check at this level: Name a case not for video. Model answer: Emergency such as chest pain. Cover rota and training.
Pilot and improve

L7: learner can audit a clinic for privacy and access. Focus module: Pilot and improve (Create, 3 h). Test with real steps before scaling. Key points: Run 10 mock visits; measure wait, success, satisfaction. Fix top problems; set a target such as 90% of calls start on time. Plan monthly reviews.

Teach: open with the worked example. First pilot: 7 of 10 on time; after fixing the link emails, 9 of 10. Then set the activity: Present your pilot review. Mark against the standard: Numbers are real and a next step is dated. Check at this level: Why keep access logs? Model answer: To show who saw a record. Peer audit.
